children: Quantum computing is no longer science fiction, and the reality check has arrived. As the industry nears commercial viability in the coming years, earnings reports that were once viewed as inconsequential are drawing heightened scrutiny.

That attention cuts both ways: When companies deliver, investors reward them. Shares of both IonQ and Quantinuum surged more than 20% on Friday in the wake of their third-quarter reports, easily outperforming a muted market rebound after artificial-intelligence panic knocked 5.5% off the Nasdaq Composite in the previous session.

'In spite of what the stock moves may suggest, strong results were largely expected. As Barron's previously reported, IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi has set the bar high for the company he helped take public back in 2021, steadily compounding revenue each quarter while targeting a $1 billion annual run rate before 2030 in what would be an industry first.

As investors continue to question when "useful" quantum systems will reach commercial scale, record revenue at IonQ was an encouraging sign. As Jefferies analyst Kevin Garrigan pointed out, demand for IonQ's systems is outpacing supply, with capacity for Superion — IonQ's latest-generation computer — sold out through 2027.

More broadly, the beat-and-raise quarter "reinforces our view that quantum demand is moving from experimentation toward commercial deployment," Garrigan wrote. Crucially for IonQ, profitability is looking increasingly within reach as operations expand, with Garrigan noting that the "central debate has shifted from whether demand exists to how quickly IonQ can expand supply, convert backlog, and scale profitably."

For Quantinuum, it was only the second earnings release since its historic initial public offering, but the results showed sustained execution from a player frequently touted as a top Wall Street pick. Following the report, Garrigan highlighted that Quantinuum was "pairing commercial momentum with a widening technical lead," dubbing it the firm's "preferred quantum name."

Morgan Stanley, which previously dubbed Quantinuum its "top quantum play," noted that new engagements with Johnson & Johnson and GE Vernova during the quarter signal "growing customer confidence" in the company's technical roadmap. That plan includes deploying a fully error-corrected system by 2029. While analysts don't expect linear growth, "the commercial and technical datapoints both moved in the right direction this quarter," they wrote.

Now, with more earnings on deck, the key question isn't just the numbers themselves, but whether companies can continue growing revenue. Both D-Wave Quantum and Rigetti Computing — two of the most-watched quantum pure plays — are set to report third-quarter results on Nov. 10.
D-Wave became the first company to get its technology to market in 2011, but its early lead has since been eclipsed by peers including IonQ, Quantinuum, and recently public Infleqtion.

That weakness showed in the second quarter. Revenue missed estimates by about $1 million — and while bulls might argue that consensus figures mean little as Wall Street only begins warming to quantum stocks, other concerns loom, notably the persistent "lumpiness" in D-Wave's results.

Much of the company's revenue is tied to inconsistent, big-ticket system sales. As the race toward commercialization accelerates, the market will likely punish that unpredictability more harshly as peers prove they can deliver steady growth.

Rigetti, meanwhile, is just beginning to bring its systems to market. With an earlier technical setback behind it, focus has shifted to hardware deliveries. Announcements of new enterprise deals are unlikely given the quiet quarter, but a steady trickle of hardware sales this year — after none in 2025 — still represents a step forward. For now, attention is centered around a $8.4 million system delivery to India's Centre for Development of Advanced Computing, which is slated for revenue recognition in the fourth quarter.
